added: Washing hands, filling glasses and pots, rinsing produce, doing dishes — the kitchen sink sees a lot of action. So, a clog, a leaky faucet or drain, or some other problem can be a real disruption to your daily life. There are lots of ways a kitchen sink can break, and at least as many ways to fix one. Some will require a plumber’s expertise, but you can handle many of the common issues yourself. You can even fix the problem by ripping the sink out and starting fresh!
===Fixing a Leaky Drain===

#Check the drain pipe connections. If you can’t see where the leak is coming from, press a clean tissue around each drain pipe connection in your under-sink cabinet while the water is running. If you find the culprit, try tightening the connection firmly but not excessively, by hand for PVC nuts or with a wrench for metal nuts. If that doesn’t work, try disconnecting and reconnecting, and potentially replacing, the pipes and/or nuts.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/plumbing/how-to-replace-a-kitchen-sink-basket-strainer/view-all/</ref>[[Image:Fix Your Kitchen Sink Step 11 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*If you have old metal drain pipes covered in rust, you should consider replacing them. Check the rusted areas for leaks since this is commonly where they're found.

#Test the sink strainer for leaks. If the drain pipe isn’t leaking, plug the sink, fill it with water, and wait 5-10 minutes. Run a clean tissue around the underside of the sink where it meets the metal sink drain, which is also known as a sink strainer.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/plumbing/how-to-replace-a-kitchen-sink-basket-strainer/view-all/</ref>[[Image:Fix Your Kitchen Sink Step 12 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Identify your sink strainer and its connectors. The metal sink strainer uses pressure connections to create a watertight seal around the sink opening from above and below. There are three main types of sink strainers: locknut, locknut with screws, and bell washer. Consult the manufacturer’s instructions or online resources on [[Remove a Kitchen Sink Drain|identifying the strainer type and the locknut or bell housing]] that holds it in place.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/plumbing/how-to-replace-a-kitchen-sink-basket-strainer/view-all/</ref>[[Image:Fix Your Kitchen Sink Step 13 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Tighten up the sink strainer connectors you’ve identified. If the locknut or bell housing feels a bit loose, try tightening it -- securely but not excessively -- and see if that stops the leak. Usually, however, a poor plumber’s putty seal is the culprit and you’ll have to pull out the sink strainer.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/plumbing/how-to-replace-a-kitchen-sink-basket-strainer/view-all/</ref>[[Image:Fix Your Kitchen Sink Step 14 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*If you're dealing with a very small leak, you may be able to fix it by applying clear silicone around the whole connection where the strainer meets the sink.

#Remove the sink strainer if it’s still leaking. After removing the locknut or bell housing that holds the strainer into place from below, press upward on the sink strainer to pop it up and out of the sink. Tap it with a rubber mallet if it needs further encouragement.<ref>https://www.todayshomeowner.com/how-to-remove-and-install-a-kitchen-sink-strainer/7/</ref>[[Image:Fix Your Kitchen Sink Step 15 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Clear away any plumber’s putty residue around the rim of the sink opening.

#Install a new sink strainer. Form a half-inch diameter ring of new plumber’s putty to place around the clean, dry rim of the sink opening. Press the new sink strainer down into the plumber’s putty firmly, and tighten the locknut or bell housing from below as per the appropriate instructions for your model.<ref>https://www.todayshomeowner.com/how-to-remove-and-install-a-kitchen-sink-strainer/7/</ref>[[Image:Fix Your Kitchen Sink Step 16 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Clear away excess putty in the sink with your fingers, a plastic putty knife, and a wet rag.
#*Test the new sink strainer by once again filling the sink, waiting several minutes, then dabbing a tissue around the connections.

#Extend and retract the auger to pull out any clogs. [[Unclog a Kitchen Sink|Feed the auger]] into the pipe opening that extends into the wall or floor. Follow the specific product instructions for extending and retracting the auger.
#*Reattach the pipes carefully, then check for leaks and proper drainage.
===Fixing a Leaky Drain===

#Check the drain connections. If you can’t see where the leak is coming from, press a clean tissue around each drain pipe connection in your undersink cabinet while the water is running. If you find the culprit, try tightening the connection firmly (but not excessively) either by hand (for PVC nuts) or with a wrench (for metal nuts). If that doesn’t work, try disconnecting and reconnecting, and potentially replacing, the pipes and/or nuts.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/plumbing/how-to-replace-a-kitchen-sink-basket-strainer/view-all/</ref>

#*If you don’t find the leak here, plug the sink, fill it with water, and wait 5-10 minutes. Run a clean tissue around the underside of the sink where it meets the metal sink drain (often called the sink strainer).

#Identify your sink strainer and its connectors. The metal sink strainer (or sink drain) uses pressure connections to create a watertight seal around the sink opening from above and below. There are three main types of sink strainers: locknut, locknut with screws, and bell washer. Consult [[Remove a Kitchen Sink Drain|How to Remove a Kitchen Sink Drain]] for instructions on identifying the strainer type and loosening the locknut or bell housing that holds it in place.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/plumbing/how-to-replace-a-kitchen-sink-basket-strainer/view-all/</ref>

#*If the locknut or bell housing feels a bit loose, try tightening it (securely but not excessively) and see if that stops the leak. Usually, however, a poor plumber’s putty seal is the culprit and you’ll have to pull out the sink strainer.

#Reinstall your sink strainer, or install a new one. After removing the locknut or bell housing that holds the strainer into place from below, press upward on the sink strainer (tap it with a mallet if needed) to pop it up and out of the sink.<ref>https://www.todayshomeowner.com/how-to-remove-and-install-a-kitchen-sink-strainer/7/</ref>
#*Clear away any plumber’s putty residue around the rim of the sink opening. Then, form a half-inch diameter ring of new plumber’s putty to place around the clean, dry rim.

#*Press the sink strainer down into the plumber’s putty firmly, and tighten the locknut or bell housing from below as per the appropriate instructions. Clear away excess putty in the sink with your fingers, a plastic putty knife, and a wet rag.
===Repairing a Leaky Faucet===

#Take preventative measures before tearing apart your faucet. Nothing will ruin a [[Fix-a-Leaky-Faucet|quick faucet fix]] like losing a tiny but critical part down the drain, scratching up the chrome finish with your wrench, or unleashing a geyser of water that soaks your entire kitchen. Taking a few simple measures beforehand can save you a lot of time and trouble afterward.<ref>http://www.thisoldhouse.com/toh/article/0,,193895,00.html</ref> #*Turn off the water to the faucet. There should be two shut-off valves beneath the sink, one each for hot and cold. Turn the faucet handles to make sure both hot and cold are off, and to get rid of excess water in the lines.
#*Plug up the drain with a stopper or rag. You don’t want to lose anything down there during disassembly!
#*Wrap the teeth of any wrench or pliers you’ll be using with a layer of duct tape. This will protect against damage to the faucet’s shiny finish.

#Replace the O-ring and/or seat washer in a compression faucet. Any kitchen faucet with separate handles for hot and cold is a compression faucet. And, most of the time, leaks are caused by faulty seat washers.<ref>http://www.thisoldhouse.com/toh/article/0,,193895,00.html</ref>
#*Remove a handle by popping off the decorative (“H” or “C”) cap and loosening the screw beneath. Repeat the whole process on the other handle as needed.
#*Use a wrench to loosen the nut that holds the stem in place. Pull out the stem.

#*Install a new O-ring (for leaky handles) or seat washer (for a leaky spout) and reassemble the handle. Both are rubber, but the O-ring is thinner. Take them to the hardware store if you need to find a match.

#Remove the handle of a single-handle faucet to investigate. Unless you already know what kind of faucet you have (either a “ball,” “cartridge,” or “ceramic disk”), you’ll need to look at the inner workings to figure it out.  Unscrew and remove the handle itself: pop the decorative cap to expose a screw, if necessary.<ref>http://www.thisoldhouse.com/toh/article/0,,193895,00.html</ref>

#*The different processes for identifying and repairing each of these three faucet types involve several steps, but the overall tools and techniques are not beyond the capability of most homeowners. Go to [[Fix-a-Leaky-Faucet|How to Fix a Leaky Faucet]] for detailed images and instructions on repairing ball, cartridge, and ceramic disk faucets.
#*That said, there’s no shame in calling a plumber if you’re not sure what you’re dealing with!
===Replacing the Entire Sink===

#Prepare your workspace. Before you [[Remove-a-Kitchen-Sink|tear out the old sink]], clear out all the cleaning bottles, buckets, pots and pans, or whatever else is in the cabinet underneath. Place old towels over the bottom of the cabinet to sop up excess water. Turn off the hot and cold water lines by turning the valves in the cabinet, then open the faucet to drain the lines.
#*If you have a garbage disposal, shut of the power to it at your main breaker panel.

#Disconnect the drain pipe and water lines. A few inches below the underside of the sink, the metal sink strainer (or sink drain) will meet the drain pipe (which will be made of either PVC or metal). Loosen the nut that connects them, either by hand (for PVC nuts) or with a wrench (for metal). There will be two of these connections if you have a double sink.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/kitchen/replace-a-sink/view-all/</ref>
#*Disconnect the hot and cold water lines (the flexible metal tubes above each shut-off valve) by loosening the nut above each valve with a wrench.

#Disconnect the [[Remove-a-Garbage-Disposal|garbage disposal]], if you’re saving it. How the disposal is connected to the sink varies based on brand and type. Refer to your product instructions or contact the manufacturer if you need guidance. The disposal will usually be connected to the drain line with either a screw or a nut.

#*Unplug the disposal, or, if it’s hard-wired, disconnect the electrical wiring to remove the disposal completely. You may also choose to lay it in the bottom of the cabinet until it’s time for re-installation.

#Cut through the sealing caulk around a top-mount sink. If your sink has a metal lip around its edge that keeps it in place, you have a top-mount. Run a utility knife around the perimeter to slice through the caulk. Work carefully if you’re not also replacing the countertop.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/kitchen/replace-a-sink/view-all/</ref>

#Remove the brackets from beneath for an undermount sink. If your sink has no lip that sits on the countertop, it is an undermount that is held up from below by a series of brackets or clips. First, cut through the caulk seal by carefully running your utility knife around the top of the sink basin, where it meets the countertop.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/kitchen/replace-a-sink/view-all/</ref>
#*Use a screwdriver to remove all the clips or brackets.
#*Removing an undermount is far easier and safer if you have a second set of hands to hold the sink while you’re working. Recruit a buddy or put your teen to work!

#Push up from underneath to lift out the sink. Once again, having a helper will make this easier, especially if you’re worried about potentially scratching up your countertop. After the old sink is out of the way, use a razor blade or putty knife to scrape away any caulk residue around the countertop opening. Be very careful if you’re keeping the countertops; if you’re not, don’t worry about it!<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/kitchen/replace-a-sink/view-all/</ref>

#Install a new sink. Essentially, you’ll be performing the removal process in reverse: apply a caulk seal, drop or lift the sink into place, tighten any clips or brackets, and fix all the water, drain, and electrical connections.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/kitchen/replace-a-sink/view-all/</ref>

#*However, you will have to install a new faucet (or re-install the old one) yourself. But with the product instructions and a little [[Install-a-Kitchen-Faucet|faucet installation help]] from wikiHow, you’ll be all set!
#*Likewise, you’ll probably need to install a new [[Remove a Kitchen Sink Drain|sink strainer]] (or sink drain), but you can handle that too!
